newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's bets on German slip for EMU, plus growth.
newsitem.headline: France's bets on German slip for EMU, plus growth.

text.p: In its bid to qualify for European monetary union the new French government is betting that Germany will miss the 3.0 percent target and that its own economy will produce enough growth to bridge any remaining gap with its neighbour.

Economists believe France will simply not limit its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, both because the Maastricht treaty does not stipulate 3.0 percent and because it would not have enough time to rectify its finances.

What counts now is by just how much Germany could overshoot, and how France balances spending discipline and measures to secure faster economic growth in 1998 so that France's public deficit eases to a reasonable level in line with Germany's.

On the growth side, Jospin may be unable to propose dramatic stimulus measures due to the conflicting commitments of not adding to the economic austerity of his centre-right predecessors and not doing anything to worsen the deficit.

"What they're saying is: 'if Germany has 3.4 percent, we'll have 3.4 percent, and if it's 3.2 percent in Germany we'll have (three point) two percent," said UBS international economist Darren Williams on Monday.
"It might not be what was first intended on fundamentals, but it is going that way," he said.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said last week France would not make the three percent mark this year and a government source said on Friday "first signs" showed it was heading for a "little over 3.4 or 3.5 percent".

He and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin have said they will not worsen the deficit, leaving them with what the government source called "narrow but manageable" room for manoeuvre in the 1998 budget, to be presented after the summer recess.

While Germany's own budget difficulties seem to be helping France to shift the consensus away from a precise 3.0 percent requirement, economists believe Jospin's hands are tied between adventurous growth-boosting measures and deficit control.
"They're trying to do several things at once. They're trying to keep voters happy, they're trying to keep the Germans happy and they're trying to keep financial markets happy," Williams said.
"What they'll probably end up doing is a bit of everything and they will end up muddling along," he said. Banking on high growth would be a "huge gamble".

High unemployment -- which rose by 32,400 in May according to data released on Monday -- and relatively weak wage growth augured badly for a Socialist-led government which saw higher consumer spending and demand as key to better growth, he said.

While Jospin is meeting his promise to discontinue civil service staff cuts, his letter on preparations for the 1998 budget tells ministers to limit running costs to the rate of inflation and to hold staff numbers next year at 1997 levels.
"People don't necessarily understand. The electorate voted for change and if anything what they get may look like more of the same," Williams said.
But things seem to be going his way on the German front.

"What doesn't surprise me is that they (France) are going for a trend evaluation. The good news for them is the Germans are possibly also tending to accept this interpretation," said David Naude at JP Morgan bank in Paris.
"The strategy now is that...3.0 percent is the objective for next year...it seems they are committed to hit it next year with better growth," said Naude.

This view won added credence at the weekend when Bundesbank governor Hans Tietmeyer, one of the Germany's main advocates of tough deficit discipline, said three percent was an "important reference number", but that sustainable deficit control was more important than one-off target achievements.

Tietmeyer's comments fit nicely with the French government line that the decision in mid-1998 on who joins the launch of the euro will be based on the trend between the results of 1997 and the forecast deficit for 1998, not on 1997 results alone.

"The interesting thing is that the strategy now is that they will stick to Maastricht and that 3.0 pct is the objective for next year -- it seems they are committed to hit it next year with better growth," said Naude.
An audit of public finances to be completed by July 21 may give a more concrete picture of the current situation.

The previous government had forecast economic growth of at least 2.3 percent this year but consumer spending indicators have offered only mixed signals so far and business investment has yet to make a long-awaited take-off.
